Reason.headline: Your brain runs on tiny batteries.
Reason.subhead: Billions of them. And they're the reason you feel sharp — or you don't.
Reason.bodyP1: Your brain is the hungriest organ you own. It never stops, and it never coasts.
Reason.bodyP2: All that energy is made by billions of microscopic batteries inside your cells — the mitochondria. When they're full and firing, you feel it. Quick. Clear. On.
Reason.bodyP3: But like every battery, they fade with time. Scientists call it mitochondrial decay. As the batteries weaken, the brain gets less of the one thing it runs on.
Reason.turn: But batteries can be looked after.
Reason.differentiation: Not at the surface. At the source.
Reason.pivot: None of this is guesswork. The roadmap came from thirty years of published research by one neuroscientist.
Reason.calloutLabel: of your body / of its energy
Reason.visualAlt: A mitochondrion glowing like a charged battery cell among dimmer, aging ones
Reason.visualCaption: Mitochondria — your brain's batteries. You have billions.

Scientist.headline: Thirty years. One question.
Scientist.subhead: Neuroscientist Dr. Jiankang Liu has spent his career on it: how does a brain keep its energy?
Scientist.bodyP1: In February 2002, three of his papers ran in a single issue of PNAS — the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, among the most respected journals in science. Most researchers never place one paper there. He placed three at once — and they have been cited more than 22,000 times since.
Scientist.bodyP2: What the papers showed, in plain words: two natural compounds — acetyl-L-carnitine and alpha-lipoic acid — restored failing mitochondria, and with them memory, in aging animals.
Scientist.bodyP3: It's a life's work — trained at UC Berkeley, carried through laboratories in the US and abroad, focused on one idea: how the brain makes its energy, and how to help it keep making it.
Scientist.bodyP4: When our founder, Mo Chen, set out to build BiGH, he didn't start with a logo or a launch plan. He started with a scientist he's known for years — and the belief that this research deserved to reach the people who need it.
Scientist.pivot: His research became a formula. We call it NuriCell.
